intro: Five more short tests on new topics — each one takes 4–12 minutes. Like Test 1, everything is pitched deliberately a little harder than the real TOEFL, so test day feels easier. You can stop midway: your answers are auto-saved on this device and restored when you come back.

sections.instructions: One dense academic passage, harder than a real TOEFL passage. Read it, then answer the questions. The passage stays on the left while you answer.
passage: When scientists first explored the deep ocean floor in the late 1970s, they expected to find a biological desert. Sunlight does not penetrate beyond about 200 meters, so photosynthesis — the process that supports nearly all life at the surface — is impossible in those depths. Instead, around cracks in the seabed where superheated water escapes from beneath the Earth's crust, researchers discovered dense communities of giant tube worms, clams, and shrimp thriving in total darkness. These hydrothermal vent ecosystems overturned a fundamental assumption of biology: that every food chain ultimately depends on the Sun. Nothing in the textbooks of the time had prepared researchers for life flourishing without light.

Vent communities rest on a different chemical foundation. Seawater seeping into the crust is heated and enriched with minerals, and it eventually erupts back into the ocean at temperatures above 350°C. Bacteria at the base of the vent food web exploit the chemical energy stored in compounds such as hydrogen sulfide, using it to convert dissolved carbon into organic matter through a process called chemosynthesis. Larger animals either graze on these bacteria or host them inside their own tissues. The giant tube worm, remarkably, possesses neither a mouth nor a digestive tract; it survives entirely on bacteria cultivated within a specialized internal organ.

Yet vent communities are as fragile as they are astonishing. An individual vent typically remains active for only a few decades before its mineral chimneys collapse or its channels become blocked, and when a vent dies, the community it supports dies with it. Unlike a surface ecosystem, a vent community cannot simply recover in place once it is lost. Vent species persist across the ocean basin only because their larvae can drift on deep currents to colonize newly formed vents, sometimes hundreds of kilometers away. This reliance on dispersal creates a new vulnerability: deep-sea mining targets precisely the mineral deposits that accumulate around vents, and destroying active sites faster than larvae can recolonize them would sever the stepping stones connecting one generation of vents to the next.

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 1–2 establish that vent ecosystems flourish without sunlight, and paragraph 3 stresses their fragility. Mining is only one detail within that second point, and photosynthesis is what vents do NOT depend on.
options: Deep-sea mining is the greatest threat facing ocean life today
Giant tube worms are the most highly evolved animals in the deep ocean
Hydrothermal vents sustain rich communities without sunlight, yet those communities are highly vulnerable
Photosynthesis supports nearly every ecosystem found in the ocean
questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?

questions.explanation: The passage states that the worm 'possesses neither a mouth nor a digestive tract' and 'survives entirely on bacteria cultivated within a specialized internal organ.' Grazing is mentioned only as what other, different animals do.
options: Bacteria cultivated in a specialized organ inside its body supply its nourishment
It grazes on bacterial mats that grow over the vent chimneys
It filters dissolved minerals directly from the heated water
It consumes smaller animals that feed on bacteria
questions.q: According to paragraph 2, how does the giant tube worm obtain food?

questions.explanation: The bacteria exploit the chemical energy in hydrogen sulfide — they use it as a resource to convert dissolved carbon into organic matter.
options: waste
measure
destroy
make use of
questions.q: The word “exploit” in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to…

questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the species persist 'only because their larvae can drift on deep currents to colonize newly formed vents,' and explicitly denies that a community can recover in place. Vents last only a few decades, not centuries.
options: individual vents remain active for centuries
their larvae can disperse to newly formed vents
mining companies avoid active vent sites
their communities can recover in place after a vent dies
questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that vent species survive over long periods mainly because…

questions.explanation: Mining is introduced as a threat that could destroy vent sites 'faster than larvae can recolonize them,' severing the stepping stones between vent generations — the dispersal chain the whole paragraph is about.
options: To explain how mineral chimneys collapse over time
To compare vent ecosystems with surface ecosystems
To show how human activity could break the chain of dispersal that vent species depend on
To argue that deep-sea minerals are more valuable than marine life
questions.q: Why does the author mention deep-sea mining in paragraph 3?

sections.title: Reading Sprint — Hydrothermal Vents

sections.instructions: Six words that appear constantly in TOEFL lectures and in university reading. Choose the closest meaning in context.

questions.explanation: To fluctuate is to rise and fall irregularly — the sentence stresses repeated rising and falling, not a single drop.
options: remained constant
changed irregularly
dropped sharply once
was measured
questions.q: “The patient's temperature fluctuated throughout the night, rising and falling several times before it finally stabilized.” — Fluctuated is closest in meaning to…

questions.explanation: To inhibit is to slow down or prevent a process — here, the chemicals stop seedlings from growing.
options: speed up
measure
hinder
replace
questions.q: “Certain chemicals in the soil inhibit the growth of seedlings, which is why so few plants survive near the factory.” — Inhibit is closest in meaning to…

questions.explanation: Plausible means something appears reasonable or likely to be true — which is why the investigators take it seriously but still ask for evidence.
options: seemingly believable
deliberately misleading
extremely detailed
impossible to verify
questions.q: “His explanation sounds plausible, but the investigators still wanted physical evidence before accepting it.” — Plausible is closest in meaning to…

questions.explanation: To deteriorate is to decline in quality or condition over time — the opposite of growing stronger.
options: expand
be inspected
grow stronger
become worse in condition
questions.q: “Without regular maintenance, the bridge's steel structure will deteriorate and eventually become unsafe.” — Deteriorate is closest in meaning to…

questions.explanation: Conspicuous means clearly visible and attracting attention — the plumage is noticed by mates and predators alike, so it cannot be camouflage.
options: rarely seen
easily noticed
well camouflaged
silent
questions.q: “The male bird's bright red plumage makes it conspicuous, which attracts mates but also draws the attention of predators.” — Conspicuous is closest in meaning to…

questions.explanation: Subsequent means coming after something in time — the attempts that followed the first, failed one.
options: earlier
secret
following
unsuccessful
questions.q: “The first expedition failed to reach the summit, but subsequent attempts succeeded.” — Subsequent is closest in meaning to…

sections.title: Vocabulary in Context — Academic Words

sections.instructions: Listen once without pausing, like the real test. Take notes. You can replay once before answering.

questions.explanation: The whole lecture develops one idea: memories are stabilized — consolidated — during sleep. Exams and word pairs appear only as examples of that process.
options: Why students often perform badly in exams
How sleep helps the brain consolidate memories
The differences between the stages of dreaming
How word pairs are used in memory research
questions.q: What is the main topic of the lecture?

questions.explanation: Direct detail: 'Twelve hours later, the group that had slept recalled significantly more of the pairs.'
options: Both groups recalled the same number of pairs
The group that stayed awake recalled more pairs
The group that slept recalled significantly more pairs
Neither group was able to recall any pairs
questions.q: According to the lecture, what happened in the word-pair experiment?

questions.explanation: The experiment is introduced right after the claim that the brain consolidates memories during sleep — it is the evidence offered for that claim, not a criticism of research methods.
options: To give evidence that sleeping after learning strengthens recall
To criticize how memory experiments are usually designed
To describe the professor's own study habits as a student
To explain why word lists are difficult to memorize
questions.q: Why does the professor mention the word-pair experiment?

questions.explanation: The professor calls the all-night session 'usually counterproductive' because 'without sleep your brain never gets the opportunity to consolidate' what was studied.
options: They are the most efficient way to prepare for an exam
They are helpful only for emotional memories
They are usually counterproductive because the brain cannot consolidate learning without sleep
They are harmless as long as they are followed by a long sleep
questions.q: What does the professor conclude about all-night study sessions?

sections.title: Listening Lab — Sleep and Memory
sections.transcript: Today I want to talk about something all of you have experienced. You study hard the night before an exam, you sleep badly, and the next day the material feels strangely fragile — as if it were never properly learned. There is a reason for that. Memory is not fully formed at the moment we learn something. Instead, the brain consolidates memories — it stabilizes them — largely during sleep. In one well-known experiment, two groups of volunteers learned a list of word pairs. One group slept within a few hours of learning; the other group stayed awake for the same length of time. Twelve hours later, the group that had slept recalled significantly more of the pairs. And it is not just the total amount of sleep that matters. The deeper stages of sleep appear to be especially important for factual material, while dream-rich sleep seems to support skills and emotional memories. So the practical implication is this: an all-night study session is usually counterproductive. You may take in more information, but without sleep your brain never gets the opportunity to consolidate it. If you remember one thing from today's lecture, make it this — study, and then sleep on it. Literally.

sections.instructions: The grammar patterns TOEFL Writing and Reading reward: modifiers, agreement, the subjunctive, and precise revision.

questions.explanation: The opening phrase 'Walking through the archive' must modify the person doing the walking — the researcher. In options A and C the documents appear to be walking, which is a dangling modifier.
options: Walking through the archive, the documents appeared disorganized.
Walking through the archive, the researcher found the documents disorganized.
Walking through the archive, the documents were found by the researcher disorganized.
Walking through the archive, disorganized documents were everywhere found.
questions.q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:

questions.explanation: Correlative conjunctions (not only … but also) require parallel forms. 'Reduce costs' is a base verb + noun, so the matching completion is 'improve efficiency.'
options: improving efficiency
efficiency improvements
improve efficiency
to improving efficiency
questions.q: Choose the best completion: “The new policy will not only reduce costs but also ___.”

questions.explanation: The subject is 'collection' (singular), not 'manuscripts.' The phrase 'of rare manuscripts' in between does not change the number, so the verb must be singular: 'was donated.'
options: The collection of rare manuscripts was donated to the university library.
The collection of rare manuscripts were donated to the university library.
The collection of rare manuscripts have been donated to the university library.
The collection of rare manuscripts are donated to the university library.
questions.q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:

questions.explanation: After verbs of demand or insistence, formal English uses the subjunctive: 'that the report be submitted' — the base form 'be,' with no tense marking.
options: The committee insisted that the report is submitted by Friday.
The committee insisted that the report was submitted by Friday.
The committee insisted that the report will submit by Friday.
The committee insisted that the report be submitted by Friday.
questions.q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:

questions.explanation: Option C uses a reduced relative clause: 'published in the journal' is short for 'which were published in the journal.' Option A uses the wrong participle, B drops the verb 'were,' and D reverses who surprised whom.
options: The results publishing in the journal surprised many experts.
The results, which published in the journal, surprised many experts.
The results published in the journal surprised many experts.
Published in the journal, many experts surprised the results.
questions.q: Combine into ONE sentence: “The results were published in the journal. The results surprised many experts.” Best version:

sections.title: Sentence Structure — Academic Style

checklist: Paragraph 1: supporters' view, in your own words
Paragraph 2: critics' concerns + one specific detail (single-species plantations that die young, or planting used as an excuse to keep emitting)
Paragraph 3: your conclusion — is tree planting worthwhile, and under what condition?
Use linking words: however, furthermore, consequently, in conclusion
sections.instructions: Read the short text, then write a response that uses it. Aim for 150–200 words.
modelAnswer: Supporters of large-scale tree planting present it as the most affordable and natural method of removing carbon dioxide from the air. They also emphasize its additional benefits: trees limit soil erosion, lower temperatures in cities, provide habitats for wildlife, and create employment in the communities that plant and maintain them.

Critics, however, argue that many campaigns are far less effective than they appear. Plantations often consist of a single fast-growing species, store relatively little carbon, and frequently die within a few years. More seriously, critics claim that planting schemes allow companies to present a green image while continuing to emit greenhouse gases rather than reducing them at the source.

In conclusion, tree planting seems worthwhile, but only as a complement to cutting emissions, never as a substitute for it. Planting must follow reductions in emissions in priority, not compete with them for funding and public attention. If diverse native species are planted and protected until they reach maturity, campaigns can deliver real benefits; without those conditions, they risk becoming little more than public relations.
passage: Supporters of large-scale tree-planting campaigns argue that planting trees is the cheapest and most natural way to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Trees, they point out, also prevent soil erosion, cool overheated cities, and create habitats for wildlife, and planting programs can provide employment for local communities. Critics respond that many campaigns plant a single fast-growing species, and that such plantations store relatively little carbon and often die within a few years. They add that tree planting can become an excuse for companies to continue emitting greenhouse gases instead of reducing those emissions at the source.
sections.selfScoreGuide: 1 = ideas unclear · 3 = clear, some errors, both views covered · 5 = clear, well-organized, accurate, own words throughout
sections.task: Summarize the supporters' view, then explain the critics' main concerns and give your own conclusion. Use your own words — do not copy sentences from the reading.
